## The problem

R and C++ leave a function differently:

- A C++ exception walks back through C++ code and runs destructors.
- An R error jumps directly back to R. C++ destructors in its path do not run.

An R error is always possible when calling R. Allocation can fail, an interrupt
can arrive, and a warning becomes an error under `options(warn = 2)`.

Across package boundaries, `charport` uses R's `Rf_error()` and long-jump
mechanism. Every R package can report these errors without depending on Rcpp,
cpp11, or another C++ framework.

Inside C++ code, `charport` temporarily turns that R jump into a C++ exception.
Destructors run, and the original R error then continues. Rcpp and cpp11
perform this bridge differently, which is why `charport` selects a
compile-time adapter for each entry style.

The reverse direction is simpler: a C++ exception must not leave through a C
entry point. The outer boundary lets C++ clean up, copies the exception message,
and only then reports an R error on the main thread.

## Choose the entry style

| R enters through | Include | Outer error boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Hand-written `.Call` | `charport.h` | `charport::r_boundary()` |
| Rcpp generated wrapper | `charport/rcpp.h` | Generated by Rcpp |
| cpp11 generated wrapper | `charport/cpp11.h` | Generated by cpp11 |

Reader construction and Builder wrapping use the selected adapter internally.
Their ordinary use is the same in all three cases:

``` cpp
charport::Reader input(x);
charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());

for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
  output.set(i, input[i]);
}

return output.to_sexp();
```

### Hand-written `.Call`

A hand-written entry point supplies its own outer boundary:

``` cpp
#include "charport.h"

extern "C" SEXP C_copy(SEXP x) {
  return charport::r_boundary("copy", [&]() -> SEXP {
    charport::Reader input(x);
    charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());
    for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
      output.set(i, input[i]);
    }
    return output.to_sexp();
  });
}
```

Put the boundary before C++ objects that need cleanup. For another raw R call,
protect only that call:

``` cpp
return charport::unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
  return Rf_eval(expression, environment);
});
```

### Rcpp and cpp11

Use `charport/rcpp.h` in a function exported by Rcpp, or `charport/cpp11.h` in a
function registered by cpp11. Do not add `r_boundary()`; the generated wrapper
already performs that job. `charport::unwind_protect()` uses the framework
selected by the header.

## Keep protected calls narrow

Objects that need destruction must live outside the protected callback:

``` cpp
Resource resource;

charport::unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
  return one_R_call();
});
```

Do not construct such an object inside the callback and then call R. An R error
would jump over that object's destructor before it could be turned into a C++
exception.

`charport`'s callback trampoline catches ordinary C++ exceptions and rethrows
them after returning through R's C code. This avoids sending a C++ exception
through C. It cannot recover a destructor that an R jump has already skipped.

## Provider initialization

A consumer can clean its own `Reader` and Builder objects. It cannot clean C++
objects created inside another package's `init(SEXP)` callback. Each package
must protect the objects it owns.

Provider initialization is a direct C callback, so it has no generated Rcpp or
cpp11 wrapper. If it owns C++ resources or calls R, use the provider boundary:

``` cpp
void * reader_init(SEXP x) {
  return charport::reader_init_boundary("yourpkg reader init", [&]() {
    std::unique_ptr<State> state(new State(x));

    charport::provider_unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
      return one_R_call();
    });

    return state.release();
  });
}
```

This runs provider destructors before continuing an R error and converts a C++
exception to an R error only after leaving the C++ catch. Range, indexed, and
release callbacks should not call R or throw exceptions.

## Worker threads

R calls and R errors stay on the main thread. Workers may do C++ work and report
C++ exceptions. Catch a worker exception, join every worker, and rethrow it on
the main thread. The outer boundary then reports it to R after cleanup.

## Where protection runs

There is no protection around Reader range access, indexed access, scalar
access, or worker loops. The fixed-cost bridge is used for Reader initialization,
final Builder wrapping, and explicit calls to `charport::unwind_protect()`.
